title: The Temple's Furnishings: Altar, Sea, and Lampstands
summary: The chapter lists the furnishings of the temple. In the courts stand a huge bronze altar, a great cast-metal basin called the Sea resting on twelve bronze oxen, and ten smaller basins for washing. Inside are ten gold lampstands, ten tables, the golden incense altar, and gold utensils, while Huram-abi's bronze work is summarized and said to be beyond weighing.
story: Chapter 3 described the structure of the temple; this chapter fills it. The movement is again from outside inward: first the bronze objects in the courtyard where the people gathered and sacrifices were offered, then the gold furnishings inside the sanctuary. With the building and its equipment complete, the stage is set for chapter 5, when the ark will be brought up and the glory of the LORD will fill the house. For the Chronicler's readers, whose second temple lacked much of this splendor (Solomon's bronze pieces had been broken up and carried to Babylon, 2 Kings 25:13-17), this list was a memory of what had been and a statement of what worship was meant to be.
historical:
The parallel account in 1 Kings 7:13-51 describes the same objects in more detail, especially the ornate wheeled stands for the basins. The Chronicler adds the great bronze altar in verse 1, which Kings mentions only in passing (1 Kings 8:64). At twenty cubits square and ten high, about thirty feet by thirty by fifteen (roughly nine by nine by four and a half meters), it was far larger than the tabernacle's altar and must have been approached by steps or a ramp.

Verse 17 says the bronze was cast in clay molds in the Jordan Valley between Succoth and Zeredah (Kings has Zarethan). The valley's clay soils suited large-scale metal casting, and archaeologists have found evidence of ancient metalworking in the region. Casting a basin of this size in one piece would have been a major technical achievement for the period.
cultural:
Water for washing was essential to Israel's worship because approaching a holy God required ritual cleanness. The tabernacle had a single bronze basin where priests washed their hands and feet before serving (Exodus 30:17-21). The temple multiplied this: the great Sea, holding three thousand baths (a bath was a liquid measure often estimated at around 22 liters or about 6 gallons, though estimates vary), for the priests' washing, and ten smaller basins for rinsing the parts of the burnt offerings (verse 6).

The name "Sea" may carry symbolism. In the mythologies of Israel's neighbors, the sea was a chaotic power, and in Canaanite texts from Ugarit Yam (Sea) is a god defeated by the storm god Baal. In Israel's temple the sea is a bronze basin, made by human hands, resting on twelve oxen and serving God's priests. Many interpreters see here a quiet claim that the LORD rules the waters, though the text doesn't spell it out. The twelve oxen, three facing each direction, may suggest the twelve tribes or the whole earth, but the text gives no interpretation. The tabernacle had one lampstand and one table for the bread of the Presence; Solomon's temple has ten of each (verses 7-8), multiplying the light and bread before God.
literary: The chapter is a catalog, and its form is part of its meaning. It moves from the courtyard to the sanctuary, from bronze to gold, from the common to the most holy. Verses 1 to 10 list items as Solomon made them; verses 11 to 18 summarize the bronze work of Huram-abi in an inventory that repeats much of chapter 3 and verses 2 to 6; verses 19 to 22 list the gold furnishings inside. The repetition of "he made" (the Hebrew verb appears thirteen times) stresses the work of building. The phrase “as prescribed” (verse 20) and the reference to the lampstands being made “according to their specifications” (verse 7) tie the temple to the law of Moses: this is not innovation but faithful elaboration of the tabernacle pattern.

doctrines.note: The progression from bronze in the courtyard to gold in the sanctuary, and the provision for washing before service, teach that nearness to God requires cleansing. Israel's worship took seriously the distance between the holy and the unclean.
The great bronze altar dominated the courtyard. Every worshiper who entered saw first the place of sacrifice. Access to God began there.

The lampstands burning before the inner sanctuary and the bread of the Presence set on the tables pictured Israel's continual life before God and his steady provision for them: light kept burning and bread laid out, day after day.

words.note: Yam, sea. The usual word for the Mediterranean or any large body of water, and in poetry often a symbol of chaos subdued by God (Psalm 93:3-4). Here it names a bronze basin, the largest object in the temple courts. The choice of name invites reflection on God's rule over the waters.

Kiyyor, basin or laver. The same word names the tabernacle's bronze basin in Exodus 30. Solomon's ten basins served a practical need (rinsing the sacrifices), but they continue the tabernacle's lesson that God's servants must be clean.

Menorah, lampstand. The tabernacle's single seven-branched lampstand (Exodus 25:31-40) became the symbol of Jewish worship. Solomon made ten. The menorah later appears in carvings of the Roman triumph over Jerusalem on the Arch of Titus in Rome.

Lechem, bread or food. The “Bread of the Presence” (verse 19), literally bread of the face, was set before the LORD on the tables and replaced every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5-9). It pictured Israel's life laid before God and God's provision for his people.

christ: Hebrews explains that the sanctuary and its furnishings, the lampstand, the table, the bread of the Presence, and the altar, were a copy and shadow of heavenly things, and that Christ entered not a sanctuary made with hands but heaven itself (Hebrews 9:1-12, 24). The objects in this chapter are therefore read in the New Testament as pointers to what Christ would accomplish. The altar of sacrifice finds its fulfillment in his once-for-all offering. The washing basins stand behind the New Testament language of believers having hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water (Hebrews 10:22). Jesus' words that he is the bread of life (John 6:35) and the light of the world (John 8:12) draw on images these furnishings kept before Israel, though Jesus is drawing on the wider biblical use of bread and light rather than on this chapter specifically. Revelation's vision of a sea of glass before God's throne (Revelation 4:6) may also echo the temple's Sea. These connections are thematic and typological, not predictions in the chapter itself.

hard.q: Does verse 2 say that pi equals three, and why do Kings and Chronicles give the Sea's capacity differently?
hard.a:
Verse 2 gives the Sea a diameter of ten cubits and a circumference of thirty, a ratio of exactly three rather than about 3.14. Skeptics have sometimes cited this as a mathematical error. Most interpreters answer that the figures are round numbers, as ancient measurements usually were, and that verse 5 says the rim was a handbreadth thick and flared like a lily: the diameter may have been measured across the outer rim and the circumference around the body below it, which would bring the numbers close to the true ratio. In any case the text is giving a builder's description, not a lesson in geometry.

The capacity also differs: 1 Kings 7:26 says the Sea held two thousand baths, and verse 5 here says three thousand. Suggested explanations include a copying error in one of the numbers, different sizes of the bath measure in different periods, or one figure recording what the Sea usually held and the other its full capacity. The difference is real, and no single explanation has won general agreement. It doesn't affect anything the chapter teaches.

questions: Every worshiper passed the altar of sacrifice before reaching the sanctuary. What does it mean that the approach to God begins with sacrifice?
The priests had to wash before they served. What does cleansing look like in the life of someone who serves God today?
The lamps were to burn and the bread was to be set out continually. What practices keep your life before God day after day?
